blocks.text: DNA to solve criminal cases. Forensic genealogists are like the private detectives of science.
They combine evidence gathered by traditional methods with DNA data, using the family tree to identify a suspect in a crime, a birth mother of an unwanted child or an adoptee.
The cases genealogists help solve can be big.

Last year, for example, a forensic genealogist was able to use DNA to help the FBI close the 26-year-old case of the "Northwest Three," the last unknown members of a serial-murdering clan that killed nine people in four states.
In 1976, the crime wave ended after a pregnant woman spotted a suspicious van and escaped with her baby girl; the baby was adopted.
Genealogy can also be helpful in smaller cases.
Genealogists in Washington recently helped to identify a woman who disappeared 25 years ago, and the FBI linked the suspect to a cold case in Massachusetts.
In an era when DNA tests are available in drugstore and on television, why would someone bother to turn to a forensic genealogist?

"I've been told it can be cheaper to use a genealogist than to conduct one's own search," says Linda Abrams of Heritage Quest in Falls Church, Va., an organization that specializes in tracing family trees.
She added, "I think people recognize that forensic genealogy is a science.
They believe in the results." Unlike genealogists working for family histories, forensic genealogists work from a specific request.
They are generally called in at the start of a case or after it has gone cold.
In the beginning, a genealogist spends some time reviewing the case file for clues -- newspaper clippings, missing persons posters, the type of case and even the suspect's age and ethnicity.
